newsitem.title: UK: Convergence trades pile on after EU budget pact.
newsitem.headline: Convergence trades pile on after EU budget pact.

text.p: Convergence trades were the order of the day after news from the EU summit in Dublin that all 15 countries had agreed on a stability pact to maintain fiscal discipline after monetary union in 1999.

The agreement was that a fall in economic growth of two percent or more of GDP would be considered to be exceptional enough for a country to avoid fines if they broke they broke the three percent deficit criteria.
If the fall in GDP was between 0.75 percent and two percent, fines would become a political decision and ministers could rule on whether fines should be levied.

"There is an element of automatic fines which the Germans were looking for, the alleviation of them at two percent, and the notion of a political deal between minus 0.75 and 2.00 to keep the French happy," said Stephen King, international economist at HSBC Markets.
"It's a classic European compromise but it will be very helpful in terms of convergence trades because it just makes the whole thing (monetary union) more likely to go ahead."
The mark sank across the board after news with mark/Paris dropping to a low of 3.3719 from 3.3780 and mark/lira dipping to 3.3719 from around 989.00 before the accord was reached.
"The market has only slowly reacted to this so far because most people weren't expecting to trade on the result until Monday, said Avinash Persaud, head of currency research at JP Morgan in Europe.

"This will prove very negative for the mark, especially against the lira and peseta and the fact that the market has only reacted slowly means there is the potential for a prolonged and significant reaction," he added.

Analysts said what they, and the market, will start doing over the course of the next few days is to put together long-term projections of budget deficits. This will help establish which countries will be able to avoid fines in the first two or three years of EMU.

They said for the stability pact to work properly countries will have to target deficits at 1.0 to 1.5 percent of GDP. Targeting 3.0 percent is not good enough as it would leave countries vulnerable to fines if they make even slight slip-ups in economic growth projections.
Outside of Europe the dollar, Swiss franc and yen should also gain on the mark, analysts said.
But the scale of gains will depend on how the market interprets the stability pact.
If it sees it simply as a device to help achieve a wide EMU then the dollar could break higher on the mark.
If it is taken at face value it will be seen as a device that reduces the policy uncertainty attached to the euro and mark weakness will be limited.
